locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Dalby. Farm, feedlot and gas field storage delivered onto Western Downs black soil. Call 1300 467 776.
locations.line: Black soil decides more about a Dalby delivery than the container ever will. Vertosol opens into cracks in October that will swallow a fence dropper, and it carries almost anything you drive across it. Put fifty millimetres of rain through it and the top of it turns to a grease that packs solid into a tyre tread and stops it doing its job. A paddock track that carried a truck at nine can be a bad idea by two in the afternoon. We plan Dalby runs around that rather than pretending it does not happen.
locations.uses: chemical, spray and drum storage on the grain and cotton country out through Cecil Plains, Jimbour and Macalister, tool and spare parts lock-ups at the feedlots north and west of town, laydown and consumables storage for gas field service crews working around Kogan, Kupunn and Condamine, a shed in a box on rural blocks where the machinery shed filled up a decade ago, site storage for builders working the residential streets in Dalby and Jandowae, and seed, fertiliser and fencing gear kept off the ground and out of the weather
access: Dalby town is one of the easier deliveries on the Downs. The streets are wide, the layout is a grid with room for a rigid truck to stand and set up, and most blocks have a gate a bed can actually get through. What changes the job is which side of the front gate you are on and what the sky has been doing. The country around town is cracking black clay. In a dry spring it opens up and carries anything. After a decent fall, the top hundred and fifty millimetres turns to grease, packs into a tread and stops it gripping, and a track that carried a header last week will not carry a loaded rigid truck today. It does not have to be raining when we arrive. It only has to have rained since. Beyond the wet, it is the ordinary Western Downs details we ask about. Farm entrances built for a header and a chaser bin are usually generous, but plenty of them have an irrigation channel, a headland drain or a run of siphon pipe alongside. The gilgai country north toward Jimbour and Macalister gives you ground that looks dead flat from the ute and is nothing of the sort at a two hundred millimetre scale, which matters a great deal when four corner castings have to finish at the same height. Powerlines to a pump shed or a house sit at exactly the height a lifted tilt bed wants to be. And through harvest and picking there is module and B-double traffic using the same roads and laneways you are, so a delivery window that suits you has to suit the farm as well. Tell us the approach, the ground and the time of year at the enquiry and we will bring the truck that suits it.

sections.h: The hour that turns a good track into a bad one
p: Anyone who has farmed Western Downs black soil knows the change is not gradual. The ground goes from firm to unusable in about the time it takes a storm cell to cross the paddock, and it stays that way for days after the sun comes back out, because the clay holds water rather than shedding it. That is why we ask about your approach before we commit a truck to a date, and why a Dalby booking through summer carries a bit of built-in slack. A loaded rigid truck bogged four hundred metres from the road is not a small inconvenience. It is a tractor, a chain, a chewed-up track and a wasted day for both of us, and none of it needed to happen.

The practical answer is usually simple. If the paddock or the laneway is doubtful, the container goes down on the firmest ground a truck can reach, which is often the gravel apron near the road or beside the shed, and you shift it into position with a tractor and chains when the ground comes good. That is a normal way to do it out here and there is no shame in it. The other option is to move the date. We would rather ring you two days out and say the run is going Thursday instead of Tuesday than turn up and make your problem worse. If there is a spot on the place that stays hard no matter what the season is doing, tell us about it when you book, because that is usually where the truck should be aiming.

sections.h: Feedlots, gas crews and farm storage
p: Out here a container earns its keep. The feedlots north and west of town use them for parts, veterinary supplies, mill spares and anything that needs to be locked and dry within reach of the operation rather than back in town. The gas field service contractors working through Kogan, Condamine and out toward Wandoan use them as relocatable laydown, because a container can be craned onto a truck and moved to the next job in a way a shed cannot. Farms use them for chemical drums, spare parts, seed and fencing gear, generally because the machinery shed lost its spare floor space some years ago and nobody wants to be the one who leaves the drums under a tarp again. There is a steady trade too in containers going onto blocks around Bell and Jandowae as a first building, holding the tools and the materials while a shed or a house is still a set of plans.

The two questions worth settling at the quote are size and ventilation. A 20ft is the workhorse and it fits down a farm laneway and through a stock gate more comfortably than a 40ft does. A 40ft gives you a machinery-length store and suits a yard with a straight approach off a formed road. On ventilation, black soil country swings hard between a cold night and a hot day, and a sealed steel box with warm air in it will sweat on the underside of the roof and drip on whatever is below. Vents fitted before delivery cost very little and save an argument later. Say what is going inside and we will tell you what it needs. It is a two minute conversation at the quote and it decides how well the thing works for the next twenty years.

sections.h: How a Dalby load is actually scheduled
p: The container is loaded at our Cornubia yard, runs out through Ipswich and Toowoomba, down the range and out along the Warrego. That is a solid half day of driving before anything is unloaded, which is why Dalby is a scheduled run rather than a next-day delivery. In practice we build the Downs runs around the loads already booked, so if there are two or three going to Dalby, Bell and Jandowae in the same week they travel together. That is better for you than a single dedicated truck, and it is the honest reason a lead time can move by a couple of days in either direction. The other variable is where the container has to come from. If the size and grade you want is already standing at Cornubia it goes on the next run west. If it has to be brought in first, that adds a couple of days at this end before anything starts moving.

What we need from you is the date pressure, early. A settlement, a harvest start, a shutdown, a contractor arriving on site with nowhere to put their gear. If there is a hard date we will build the run around it, and if we genuinely cannot make it we will say so at the enquiry rather than at four o'clock the day before. Ring 1300 467 776 with the address, the size you are after and a description of the approach and we can usually give you a delivery window on the same call. If the job is on a property rather than in town, have the approach ready to describe: how far in from the road, what the surface is, and whether anything on the way gets soft. It saves a second phone call and it is the difference between a firm date and a rough one.

faqs.q: How long does it take to get a container to Dalby?
faqs.a: Three to six business days is the normal window. The container comes out of our Cornubia yard south of Brisbane and travels through Toowoomba and down the range, so it is a scheduled run rather than an overnight one. What stretches it is wet weather on black soil, a crane booking, or a unit that needs vents or a lockbox fitted before it goes. If a date is locked in at your end, put it in front of us when you first ring and we will work the schedule back from it.

faqs.q: Can you put a container straight onto black soil?
faqs.a: You can, but it will not stay where you put it. Cracking clay swells and shrinks through the year and it does not do it evenly, so a container sitting directly on soil will settle one corner at a time and end up out of square, which is when the doors stop lining up. Hardwood sleepers or concrete pads under the four corner castings, checked level both ways and across both diagonals, fix it permanently for very little money. Say what the ground is when you order and the timber travels with the container.

faqs.q: Can you deliver into a feedlot or a gas site near Dalby?
faqs.a: Regularly, but those sites run on their own rules and we need to know them before the truck leaves. An induction, a gate register, PPE, a booked time slot, somebody to lead the truck through to where the container is going, and on some places a wash-down or biosecurity step on the way in. None of it is hard. All of it is hopeless to sort out with a driver idling at a boom gate. Pass on the site contact and the requirements when you book and the delivery turns into a non-event.

faqs.q: Can I look at the container before it comes out to Dalby?
faqs.a: Yes. The yard is at 51–55 Bromley Street, Cornubia, roughly half an hour south-east of the Brisbane CBD off the M1. Units sit out on hardstand, so you can walk around one, swing the doors and look down the floor for yourself rather than taking a description on faith. Give us a call before you make the trip, both so somebody can meet you and so the unit you want is not buried behind three others. We are open Monday to Friday 7:30am to 5pm and Saturday 8am to 12pm. If a day of driving is not worth it, photos of the actual container are available on request and we send them before delivery.

locations.depot: our Cornubia yard, run out along the Warrego through Toowoomba, Dalby and Warra

locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft where the approach is formed; crane truck for 40ft and for tight laneways and yards
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Chinchilla. Storage for melon farms, gas crews and brigalow blocks, with the ground and the wet allowed for.
locations.line: Two kinds of ground meet at Chinchilla and they behave nothing alike. The sandy rises carry a truck beautifully in any weather and then let a corner casting sink into them over a season. The brigalow and belah country either side is heavy clay that turns to soap after rain and will hold a bogged truck for two days while it dries out. Knowing which one your block sits on is worth more to us than any other single piece of information you can give us at the quote.
locations.uses: bin, pallet and packing gear storage on the melon country through Brigalow and Chinchilla itself, drum and chemical lock-ups on grain and cotton blocks, relocatable laydown and consumables storage for the gas field crews working the Surat Basin out toward Miles, Wandoan and Kogan, secure tool storage for the fitters, boilermakers and electricians running mobile workshops off utes and trailers, feed and fencing storage on the cattle blocks north toward the Auburn and Boyne, and a dry store on newly bought scrub blocks with no shed on them yet
access: The town is straightforward. Wide streets, an easy grid, generous industrial frontages down toward the highway and enough room for a rigid truck to stand and unload without a fuss. Out of town it splits. The sandy rises and the old cypress country give you an approach that stays firm through most of the wet, which makes them the easiest properties on the Downs to deliver to in February. The trade-off comes afterwards, because sand carries poorly under a point load and a container corner concentrates a couple of tonne into an area the size of a dinner plate. It will settle, and it will do it unevenly. The brigalow and belah blocks are the opposite arrangement. Excellent bearing when dry, useless when wet, and slow to come back because the clay holds water rather than draining it. Melon hole country adds a wrinkle that catches people out. From the seat of a ute it reads as flat. It is not, and the depressions are just deep enough and just broad enough that a truck sets up in one without anybody noticing until the bed is up and the container is not going where it was meant to. Then the ordinary details: farm gates set out for a tractor rather than a truck with a wide bed, grids on private tracks with no rating and no history, table drains that a rear wheel can drop into, and irrigation mainlines and siphon pipe alongside headlands. On gas leases and station tracks the surface is often good, formed gravel that has been maintained, and the constraint is access permission and a gate key rather than the ground. Tell us at the enquiry whether the last kilometre is sand, clay or formed gravel, and whether anything is locked.

sections.h: Sand that lets go and clay that holds on
p: The sandy rises around Chinchilla will take a truck in the middle of a wet week, which makes them a gift as far as delivery goes. What they will not do is hold a container level on their own. Sand drains fast and carries badly, so within a season or two of sitting straight on it the low corner has found its own level and the doors have started to bind. The fix is small: hardwood or concrete under each corner casting, dug in and checked on both diagonals, so the load spreads over a proper footprint instead of punching through. Do it on the day the container lands and you never think about it again. Sand also travels when water runs across it, so if the spot sits under a shed roof line with no gutter on it, either move the container or move the water.

The clay country is the reverse problem. Once it has taken up water it is genuinely unsafe to be driving a loaded truck across, and it stays that way for longer than most people expect, because brigalow soil does not shed water, it holds it. We would rather move a booking than put a truck onto it. If your place has a hard stand near the shed or a gravel apron by the road that stays firm regardless, tell us where it is and we will aim for that. Setting the container down on solid ground and letting you walk it into position with a tractor at your own pace is a perfectly normal way to do a delivery out here.

sections.h: Gas country storage that has to move again
p: A lot of the containers going into the Surat Basin are not staying anywhere permanently. A crew sets up near a lease, works it for eight or ten months, and moves on to the next one. That is exactly what a container is good at and exactly what a shed is not. It can be craned onto a truck and be at the next site the same week, it locks, it keeps dust and rain off consumables and hand tools, and it does not leave you arguing about make-good at the end of an access agreement. The same logic works further down the scale. A mobile fitter or an auto electrician running out of a ute and a trailer gets a lockable base on site, and takes it with them when the contract finishes instead of renting a shed in town they only half use.

Two things are worth thinking about at the order rather than later. First, hire against purchase. If the work has a program with an end date on it, hire keeps the asset off your books and makes the removal somebody else's problem. If the container is going to follow the crew around for years, buying is cheaper by a long way. Second, fit-out. Vents, an internal shelf line, a lockbox over the handle, a coat of paint that is not shipping-line livery if the client is fussy about how the laydown looks. All of that is easier to do here before the container leaves than out there afterwards, because out there it is a contractor, a trip and a day.

sections.h: Chinchilla travels with the Dalby run
p: Chinchilla sits about eighty kilometres past Dalby on the Warrego, and it is the far end of what we can reasonably do in a single day out of Cornubia. In practice that means Chinchilla loads travel with whatever else is going west that week, which is usually Dalby, Warra, Miles or Wandoan. Four to seven business days is the honest window. If two or three orders land together the run gets easy and the date firms up quickly. If yours is the only one, it waits for a truck heading that way, or it goes on its own and the cartage reflects that. We will tell you which of those it is when we quote, rather than giving you a date and finding a reason later.

The season matters as much as the schedule. Through the summer storms we deliberately keep a couple of days of movement in the western bookings, because putting a truck onto wet brigalow to hold a date does nobody any good. Ring 1300 467 776 with the address, the size and a rough description of the last kilometre and we will give you a realistic window on the call. It also helps to tell us if the container has to be on the ground before something else happens, whether that is a crop coming off, a crew arriving or a lease starting. Knowing the constraint is what lets us decide whether your box goes on this week's run or waits three days for a better one. Vague dates get vague answers out here. Specific ones almost always get a better result.

faqs.q: How long is delivery to Chinchilla?
faqs.a: Four to seven business days is normal. The container comes from our Cornubia yard south of Brisbane and Chinchilla is at the far end of a day's run west, so loads usually travel with other orders going to Dalby, Warra, Miles or Wandoan that week. A single container on its own can still go, it just goes as a dedicated trip. Summer storms will move a date, because we will not put a loaded truck onto wet brigalow country to hold a booking.

faqs.q: Can a container be moved again later if the job shifts?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is one of the main reasons gas field crews around here use them rather than building something. A container can be lifted onto a truck and relocated to the next site with a day's notice. Two things make it easier: leave enough clear space around it for a truck and a crane to work, and keep it level and off the ground on pads so the underside is not bedded into soil that has to be dug out before it can be lifted.

faqs.q: Will a container sink on sandy Chinchilla country?
faqs.a: On bare sand or thin turf over sand it will find its own level, and it will not do it evenly, because every corner casting drives a couple of tonne into a footprint the size of a dinner plate. That is what puts a frame out of square and starts the doors binding. Sleepers or concrete pads under each of the four corners, bedded in and checked across both diagonals, spread that load and end the problem for good. Flag the ground type on the order and the materials come out with the container.

faqs.q: Can you deliver to a property with a locked gate or a station track?
faqs.a: Yes, provided we know before the truck leaves. Locked gates, gate keys, access permissions on a lease, a grid with no rating, a track that needs a particular approach, stock that should be shifted first, or a requirement to ring ahead so somebody meets us. All of that is fine when it is arranged and a real problem when a driver finds it at four in the afternoon four hundred kilometres from the yard. Give us the details and a contact number at the booking.

locations.name: Kingaroy
locations.depot: our Cornubia yard, run north-west through Caboolture and over the Blackbutt Range on the D'Aguilar
locations.leadTime: Usually 3–6 business days, scheduled around the range run and the weather
locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft where there is a straight approach; crane truck for 40ft and for steep or terraced blocks
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Kingaroy. Peanut, hay and machinery storage on South Burnett red soil, delivered over the Blackbutt Range.
locations.line: The range comes first with Kingaroy. Whatever is going up there has to climb the D'Aguilar through Blackbutt, and a long rigid truck carrying a 40ft is a different vehicle on that road to one carrying a 20ft. After that it is the red soil and the fall of the country. Almost nothing in the South Burnett is flat. Blocks roll away from the house, driveways cut across a slope rather than running up it, and a container that is not sitting on four corners at the same height will tell you about it within a year.
locations.uses: peanut, grain and seed storage on the red soil country around Kumbia, Taabinga and Memerambi, hay and fodder kept dry and away from vermin through a wet summer, machinery parts and workshop gear on cattle and cropping blocks out toward Wooroolin and Wondai, secure storage for the vineyards and cellar doors through Moffatdale and Ficks Crossing, biosecurity-conscious storage sited outside the shed area on piggeries and poultry sheds, and lock-up storage on the lifestyle blocks and small acreage going in around Nanango and Taabinga
access: Two things shape a South Burnett delivery: the road in, and the fall on the block. The D'Aguilar climb through Blackbutt is a real range road with tight sections, a decent grade and mature timber close to the carriageway. A tilt-tray carrying a 20ft climbs it every week without drama. A longer combination carrying a 40ft is a slower and more considered exercise, and on some approaches beyond the range it is genuinely the wrong answer. Where 40ft of length matters on a block with an awkward approach, two 20ft placed end to end usually gets you more usable space and a far simpler delivery day. The second half is the ground. South Burnett red soil is deep, it is beautiful country, and it is undulating almost everywhere. Driveways here tend to be long, unsealed, and cut across a slope with a table drain on the high side, which means a loaded truck is running with a camber on it rather than sitting flat. In the dry that is fine. After rain the red soil goes slick on the surface while staying firm underneath, and a truck that loses the crown of the drive slides toward the low side. Frost is worth mentioning too. Winter mornings up here get properly cold and a shaded section of an unsealed drive can still be greasy at ten in the morning when the rest of it has dried out. On the block itself we ask about turning space at the far end, gates measured at their narrowest point rather than at the posts, powerlines running to a pump or a shed, and whether the spot the container is going has any fall across it. Almost all of these blocks are deliverable. They just need the right truck picked before the day rather than on it.

sections.h: Over the range, and what size makes it
p: The honest advice for Kingaroy is to settle the size question before anything else. The run from Cornubia goes north through Caboolture and up the D'Aguilar over the Blackbutt Range, and while that road handles heavy vehicles all day every day, it is not the same job carrying six metres of container as it is carrying twelve. Once you are past the range and onto a private driveway with a slope, a crown and a bend in it, the difference becomes obvious very quickly. A 20ft on a tilt-tray will get to almost any block in the South Burnett. A 40ft needs a straight run at the placement spot of close to twenty metres, and a driveway wide enough for the truck to line up before it starts unloading.

That is not us being difficult about it. A truck that cannot make the turn at the top of a long drive has to reverse back down a slope with a table drain on one side, and that is the sort of afternoon nobody wants. Send a photo taken from the gate looking up the drive, one of the spot itself with a bit of the surroundings in frame, and tell us roughly how much fall there is across it. That is usually enough for us to say which truck is coming and whether the size you have in mind is the right one. If the drive climbs onto a bench or crosses a table drain partway up, mention it, because that is usually where a long bed grounds out rather than at the gate.

sections.h: Peanuts, hay and keeping the moisture out
p: Most of what goes into a container around Kingaroy has to stay dry, and dry here is not only about the roof. The South Burnett gets cold clear nights and warm days for a good part of the year, and that swing is what produces condensation inside a sealed steel box. Warm moist air gets in during the afternoon, the roof panel drops below dew point overnight, and the moisture ends up on the underside of the roof and then on whatever is stacked below it. People blame the container. It is usually the ventilation. It bites hardest in the shoulder seasons, when the days are still warm and the nights have already dropped into single figures, and it catches people who have shut something away over winter without opening the doors once.

The answer is a set of vents fitted before delivery, a bit of air movement under the floor by keeping the unit up on pads rather than flat on the soil, and not stacking hay or bagged product hard against the walls where air cannot circulate. Leave a hand's width off the wall line and a gap at the door end. If you are storing seed or anything you intend to plant, that gap is the difference between opening the doors in spring to what you put in and opening them to a problem. Tell us what is going in at the quote and we will set the unit up for it rather than sending a bare box. It costs very little to get right at the start and it is the whole difference between a good store and a wasted season.

sections.h: Blocks that fall away from the house
p: Ask anybody who has poured a slab in the South Burnett how much fall there is in country that reads as gently rolling from the road. A container handles that perfectly well provided somebody deals with it on the day it lands. The whole weight runs through the four corner castings, so those four points have to finish at a common height, and on a sloping site the way there is to pack the downhill corners up on stacked hardwood or bed pads into the fall. What you should not do is bench out the uphill side. It looks neater the afternoon the truck leaves and it hands you a channel along the top wall that funnels runoff down the length of the container for the next twenty years.

Point the doors uphill if the site gives you the choice, because a pair of doors that has to be hauled against the slope every time gets old inside a month. Knock the grass back around the base and keep it back. Vegetation packed against the bottom rail holds water on the steel for weeks at a stretch, and that does more damage over time than the rain ever does to a container living outdoors. Leave the underside open so air moves through and runoff gets away rather than ponding under the floor. Where the site allows it the levelling is part of the delivery, so mention the fall when you are getting a price and the sleepers travel with the unit.

faqs.q: Can you get a 40ft container to a block near Kingaroy?
faqs.a: Often, but the approach decides it rather than the container. A 40ft needs close to twenty metres of straight, firm run at the placement spot and a driveway the truck can line up in before it starts unloading, and it is a slower job over the Blackbutt Range. On a rolling South Burnett block with a long cross-slope drive, two 20ft placed end to end usually gives you more usable space and a much easier delivery. Send a photo from the gate looking up the drive and we will tell you honestly which way it should go.

faqs.q: How long does delivery to Kingaroy take?
faqs.a: The usual window is three to six business days. The container leaves our Cornubia yard south of Brisbane and runs north through Caboolture and over the D'Aguilar, so it is a scheduled trip rather than a next-day one. Crane bookings, vents or a lockbox being fitted, and wet weather on an unsealed driveway are the usual reasons a date moves. If there is a deadline at your end, say so on the first call and the run gets planned backwards from it.

faqs.q: Will a container keep hay and seed dry through a South Burnett winter?
faqs.a: It will, provided it is ventilated and up off the ground. The cold nights and warm days here drive condensation inside any sealed steel box, and that moisture ends up on the underside of the roof and then on what is stacked below. Vents fitted before delivery, the unit sitting on pads so air moves underneath, and a gap left between the stack and the walls handles it. Cargo-worthy units are checked wind and watertight before they leave our yard, and with the ventilation sorted the contents come out in the condition they went in.

faqs.q: How do you sit a container on a sloping block at Nanango or Kumbia?
faqs.a: Yes, and you would struggle to find a block out that way without some fall on it. The method is to pack the downhill corners up to meet the uphill ones on stacked hardwood or pads bedded into the slope, rather than benching out the high side and leaving a channel for runoff to sit in against the wall. Doors face uphill where the site allows it. Set up that way, the frame carries its load the way it was built to and the doors still shut properly in twenty years.

locations.name: Roma

locations.truck: Tilt-tray for 10ft and 20ft where the approach is formed; crane truck for 40ft and for tight yards and laneways
locations.metaDesc: Shipping containers for sale and hire in Roma. Cattle, saleyard and gas field storage delivered west along the Warrego on a scheduled run.
locations.line: Roma is about six hundred kilometres of Warrego Highway from our yard, which puts it firmly in scheduled-run territory. That is the single most useful thing to understand before you order. The container is the easy part. The truck is the part that has to be going that way, and when we can put your load in with others heading to Miles, Wallumbilla, Yuleba and Mitchell the whole thing gets quicker and cheaper for everybody. Tell us your date early and we will build the run around it instead of fitting you in afterwards.
locations.uses: vet supplies, tags, drench and handling gear stored close to the yards on cattle properties through Wallumbilla, Yuleba and Injune, hay and lick storage that keeps vermin and weather out, laydown and consumables for the gas field service crews working the Surat Basin north of town, spare parts and tooling for the mobile fitters and boilermakers who keep those crews running, secure storage for the businesses along the highway frontage and the Bungil industrial area, and a lockable store on newly fenced blocks where the shed is still a plan
access: Roma town delivers well. The streets are wide, the industrial frontages out toward the highway have room to work, and a rigid truck can stand and set up in most residential streets without a fight. What we ask about is the country beyond it, because that is where the day gets decided. Properties out through Wallumbilla, Injune, Surat and the Mitchell side commonly have several kilometres of private track between the front gate and the shed, and the condition of that track is a bigger factor than anything else on the job. Formed and maintained gravel is a comfortable run. Formed earth is fine in the dry and useless within an hour of a storm. Grids come up constantly out here, and most of the private ones have no plate, no rating and nobody left on the place who remembers what went underneath them. A rigid truck under a container asks a great deal more of a grid than the ute and float it was likely built around, so where there is doubt we would sooner take a side gate, place the container on hard ground short of the crossing, or bring a crane truck, than establish the answer with a wheel through the rails. Beyond that it is the usual western list. Gates that measure narrower than they look. Room to turn at the far end, which has to be truck-sized and firm, because a tilt-tray must be square to the ground before it unloads and backing three kilometres out to the road at dusk is not a plan. Cattle in the laneway, which want shifting before a truck comes down it rather than after. Powerlines to a pump or a homestead at exactly the wrong height. And bulldust holes on a well-used track, which look like nothing and are not.

sections.h: A truck that is already heading west
p: Nearly everything about pricing and timing on a Roma delivery comes back to one question: is there already a truck going that way. Six hundred kilometres each way is a serious commitment for a single container, so we build the western runs around whatever is booked. When a Roma order can travel with loads going to Miles, Wallumbilla, Yuleba or Mitchell, the schedule tightens up and the cartage is far more sensible. When it is on its own it still goes, it just goes as a dedicated trip and the quote reflects that honestly. It also means the answer changes from week to week, which is exactly why we would rather work it out with you on the phone than publish something that will be wrong by the time you read it.

What that means for you in practice is that lead time is a window rather than a promise, and the window is genuinely five to nine business days most of the year. It also means early notice is worth real money. If you know in mid-March that you need a container on the ground by the end of April, tell us in March. We will put it on the next run heading that way rather than chartering a truck for it in the last week. If your date is fixed and immovable, say so at the enquiry, because that changes how we quote it and we would rather have that conversation up front than explain it later. Notice buys you a choice of size and grade as well, rather than whatever happens to be loadable in the week you finally ring.

sections.h: Saleyard weeks, gas crews and cattle country storage
p: Roma runs on cattle and gas, and the containers reflect it. On the properties, the common job is a lockable store near the yards for drench, tags, vaccines, spare parts and handling gear, so that a job at the yards does not become a trip back to the shed. Fodder and lick storage is the other one, especially where mice and weather have already cost somebody a season's worth. In town and on the highway frontage it is trade and business storage, and north toward Injune it is gas field laydown that has to be lockable, dustproof enough to matter and movable when the crew moves. What all of those have in common is that the container is working a long way from a supplier, so what ends up inside tends to be the gear you cannot afford to be without on a Sunday.

One local timing note worth passing on. Sale days and the weeks around them put a lot of stock transport on these roads and a lot of people in town, and it is not always the ideal morning to have a truck standing in a driveway waiting on somebody to come home and open a gate. If your week is built around the saleyards, tell us and we will aim the delivery at a day that suits you. It costs nothing to plan around and it saves the situation where a container is on the ground and the person who knows where it was supposed to go is fifty kilometres away. The same goes for shearing, branding or a contractor being on the place. Tell us the week it is happening and we will aim around it.

sections.h: Grids, gates and the last twenty kilometres
p: The most common reason a western delivery goes wrong is not the highway, it is the last twenty kilometres. Those are the ones we cannot see on a map and cannot judge from the road. A grid of unknown rating, a culvert with grass growing out of the end of it, a creek crossing that has been washed out since anybody last drove a truck over it, a gate that measures two hundred millimetres narrower than the bed needs, or a turning area at the shed that works for a tractor and not for a rigid with a container on it. None of those show up on a satellite image, and every one of them will end a delivery day that started perfectly well.

Every one of those is easy to sort out at the booking and expensive to discover on the day, because on a Roma job the day cost half a week to arrange. So we ask, and we would rather ask too much than too little. Walk the approach before you order if you have not driven it with a truck in mind. Tell us where the firm ground is. If in doubt, the fallback that works almost everywhere out here is to put the container down on the hardest surface a truck can safely reach and leave you to walk it into position with a tractor when it suits. That is a normal outcome out west, not a failure. Talk the approach through with us and we will tell you which parts of it we are actually worried about.

faqs.q: How long will it take to get a container to Roma?
faqs.a: Five to nine business days is the honest range. Roma is roughly six hundred kilometres west of our Cornubia yard, so the container travels on a scheduled western run rather than a dedicated overnight trip. When your order can travel with loads going to Miles, Wallumbilla, Yuleba or Mitchell, the date firms up quickly. If it goes on its own it becomes a dedicated trip and the quote will say so. Early notice is genuinely worth money out here.

faqs.q: Will your truck cross the grid on my property?
faqs.a: Only where we can establish what it will carry, and most private grids west of Dalby have no plate and no history anybody can vouch for. A rigid truck under a container is a far bigger ask than the ute and float the grid was probably built around. If yours is engineered and rated, say so. If nobody knows, say that instead and we will look at whether there is a side gate, whether the container can go down on hard ground short of the crossing for you to walk in with a tractor, or whether a crane truck is the cleaner answer. Any of those beats a wheel through the rails.

faqs.q: Can I get a container to a property out past Injune or Surat?
faqs.a: Yes, and we do it regularly, but it is planned rather than simply booked. The things that decide it are the condition of the private track, grids and creek crossings on the approach, whether there is genuine truck-sized turning room at the far end, and the weather in the week before. Give us the property name, the distance from the bitumen, a description of the track and a contact who will be on the place, and we will tell you what will and will not make it.

faqs.q: Can I inspect a container before it is carted out to Roma?
faqs.a: You can, though it is a long drive for most people out this way. The yard is at 51–55 Bromley Street, Cornubia, south-east of Brisbane off the M1, open Monday to Friday 7:30am to 5pm and Saturday 8am to 12pm, and the units sit out where you can swing the doors and look the floor over yourself. For a Roma buyer the practical answer is usually photographs instead. Ask for them and images of the actual unit go to you on request before delivery — corner posts, door end, roof and the floor inside.

locations.line: We will be straight about Charleville. It is not a next-day town and anybody telling you otherwise has not carted anything past Morven. This is seven hundred and fifty kilometres of Warrego from our yard, and the way it works is that your container goes out when there is a truck heading that far west. Plan for that and the whole thing goes smoothly.
locations.uses: shearing shed gear, wool packs and handling equipment stored where the work happens, drench, vaccines and animal health supplies kept out of the heat, exclusion fencing wire, posts, strainers and netting staged on blocks partway through a cluster fencing project, spare parts, filters and oils for machinery two hours from the nearest supplier, feed and lick storage that mice and cockatoos cannot get into, and secure storage for the tourism, accommodation and contracting businesses working in and around town
access: Charleville town itself is easy country for a truck. Wide streets, flat ground, generous frontages and room to set up. The complications start on the way in and on the way out to a property. The Warrego from Roma west is a good highway with long stretches of single-lane sealed section where meeting a road train means getting a wheel onto the shoulder, which is a slow business for a loaded truck and part of why a run out here takes the time it does. On the properties, the approach can be twenty kilometres of formed earth off the bitumen, and formed earth out here is superb when dry and unusable within an hour of rain. Mulga country gives you a red surface that greases up on top while staying hard underneath, so the truck loses steering before it loses traction. On the downs and channel country you get black soil that behaves like wet clay everywhere else, only there is a great deal more of it and a great deal further to walk. Bulldust is the third thing and it is genuinely dangerous rather than merely inconvenient, because a hole in a well-used track fills level with fine dust and reads as solid road right up until a front wheel drops into it. Gates, grids and floodways are the rest of it. Grids out here are old, unrated and frequently the only way in. Floodways on station tracks scour after every event and are often not the shape they were last time. Turning space at the far end has to be firm and truck-sized. Tell us the distance from the bitumen, what the surface is, and when the track last saw a grader, because a newly graded surface has nothing binding it together and will not carry a loaded truck until traffic and a bit of weather have worked it in.

sections.h: Why the date is a window, not a promise
p: There is no depot at Charleville and there is no daily freight run we can slot a container onto. What there is, most weeks, is a truck going west with a load on it, and your container travels when that happens. That is why the lead time we quote is one to two weeks rather than a number of days, and why we would much rather tell you that at the enquiry than manufacture a date and disappoint you at the far end of it. If your order can travel with something else heading to Morven, Augathella or Quilpie the timing improves. If it cannot, it either waits for the next run or goes as a dedicated trip. Either way you will know which of the two it is before anything is booked.

The way to make this work in your favour is notice. If the container is for shearing, for a fencing program, for a season or for a build, you generally know weeks out. Tell us then, and we will put it on the next suitable run rather than scrambling for a truck in the last few days. If you have an immovable date we will tell you honestly at the quote whether we can hold it. And if the answer is that the only way to hit it is a dedicated trip, you will hear that from us up front rather than reading it on an invoice. The customers who get the best out of us here are the ones who ring during the planning rather than in the week the gear is needed.

sections.h: Wet roads, and the closure that stops everything
p: Out here, rain does not just make delivery inconvenient, it makes it illegal. Unsealed roads across the western shires get closed to heavy vehicles after rain, and they stay closed until the road opens again, which can be days after the sky has cleared. That is not a decision anybody at this end gets to make and it is not something we can work around with a bit of care. When a road is shut, the container stays where it is. The other half of it is that out here there is no alternative route. There is no sealed detour to fall back on, so a closure anywhere along the approach stops the whole delivery rather than just the last leg of it. Local knowledge counts for a lot in this: if you know your access usually reopens a couple of days after a fall, tell us, because that is a far better planning input than a forecast.

So we plan for it. Through the wetter months there is deliberate slack in the western schedule, and if a road closure catches a load in transit we will ring you and tell you where things stand rather than leaving you at the gate wondering. If the delivery date matters, the practical advice is to order far enough ahead that a week of weather cannot sink the plan, and to nominate a fallback spot on the place that can be reached off the bitumen or off formed gravel. Setting a container down at the front of the property on hard ground, for you to shift in later with a tractor, is very often the sensible outcome of a wet fortnight rather than waiting another two weeks for perfect conditions.

sections.h: Get the specification right the first time
p: This is the part people who live closer to town never have to think about. When a container is going seven hundred and fifty kilometres, a change of mind after it lands is not a quick swap. So we spend more time on the order for a Charleville job than we would for a Brisbane one, and it is worth going through it properly on the phone. Size, first: a 20ft covers most station and shed jobs comfortably, a 40ft suits machinery-length storage where the approach can take it, and two 20ft is sometimes the better answer than one 40ft because they can go in two different places. The other question is doors. A single set at one end suits a store you load once and then work out of. Doors at both ends make a long unit far more usable when it has to sit hard against a fence.

Then the fit-out. Vents matter more out here than most people expect, because the temperature swing between a summer afternoon and a winter night is enormous and a sealed box will sweat. A lockbox over the handle is cheap insurance on a shed a long way from the house. Shelving, a personnel door, a coat of paint in something other than shipping-line colours, a set of tie-down points inside. All of that is a small job at our yard and a genuine expedition once the container is standing in a paddock west of Morven. Tell us what it is for and let us fit it before it goes. Have that conversation once, properly, and the container turns up ready to work rather than needing a tradesman found locally to finish it off.

faqs.q: How long does it really take to get a container to Charleville?
faqs.a: One to two weeks is the honest answer, and it depends on a truck already heading that far west. Charleville is about seven hundred and fifty kilometres from our yard and there is no daily freight run we can put a container on. If your order can travel with something going to Morven, Augathella or Quilpie the date firms up. If it needs a dedicated trip, we will tell you that at the quote. Give us as much notice as you can and the whole thing gets easier.

faqs.q: What happens if it rains before my delivery?
faqs.a: The run stops. Unsealed roads across the western shires get closed to heavy vehicles after rain and they stay closed until they dry out and reopen, which is often days after the weather clears. That is not a call we make and it is not something a careful driver can work around. There is deliberate slack in the western bookings through the wet months, and you will get a phone call telling you where your load actually is rather than being left at the gate guessing.

faqs.q: Can you deliver out to a station property west of Charleville?
faqs.a: Regularly, but it needs planning rather than just a booking. What we need is how far you are off the bitumen, what the track is made of, what shape the grids and floodways on the approach are in, whether a truck has room to turn on firm ground at the far end, and a contact who will actually be on the place. Where the last section is doubtful, the standard fallback is to leave the container on hard ground closer to the bitumen and let you bring it the rest of the way with a tractor when the track comes good.

faqs.q: Should I get vents and a lockbox fitted before it comes out?
faqs.a: Almost always, yes. Out here the swing between a hot afternoon and a cold night is severe, and a sealed steel box with warm air trapped in it will condense on the underside of the roof and drip onto what is below. Vents fitted at our yard cost very little and stop it. The same logic goes for a lockbox, shelving or a personnel door. It is a small job here and a serious exercise once the container is standing in a paddock a long way past Morven.

locations.line: Nothing about Longreach is next-day and we would rather say so plainly than have you find out. Depending on which way the freight is moving in a given fortnight, a container heads out along the Landsborough from the south-east or comes across the Capricorn from our Rockhampton depot through Emerald and Barcaldine. Either way it is over a thousand kilometres and it goes when a truck is going. One to three weeks is the real range, and a wet week in the downs country adds to it because the roads close and nothing moves at all.
locations.uses: shearing and mustering gear kept together and locked at the shed rather than scattered across a property, drench, vaccines and animal health lines stored out of the heat, spare parts, filters, belts and oils for machinery a very long way from a supplier, poly fittings, troughs and pump spares staged near the bore, fodder and lick storage that keeps birds and mice out, and secure storage for the tourism operators, contractors and small businesses working in and around town
access: The town is flat, wide and about as easy as delivery gets once a truck has actually arrived. Longreach streets have room, the industrial and highway frontages are generous, and there is no shortage of space to set up. The interesting part is the country. Mitchell grass downs are black self-mulching soil, and in the dry the surface breaks down into a loose crumbly layer over hard ground that carries a truck without complaint. Add rain and that same soil turns into something you cannot walk in, let alone drive a loaded rigid across, and it is slow to dry because there is nowhere for the water to go. That is the reason downs roads get shut to heavy vehicles after rain and stay shut, and it is why a wet week can push a Longreach delivery out further than the rain itself lasted. Station approaches are the second factor. Twenty, thirty, sometimes fifty kilometres of formed earth or gravel off the bitumen, with grids of unknown age and rating, floodways that reshape themselves after every event, and bulldust holes on the well-used sections that fill flush with the surface and read as solid until a wheel finds the bottom of one. Gates are often narrower than they look because a post has been reset at some point. Turning room at the shed has to be genuinely truck-sized and firm. There is also the plain matter of distance from help. A truck that gets into trouble ninety kilometres from town on a station track is a long, expensive problem, so the driver will be conservative, and we would rather set a container down at a hard spot short of the shed than commit to a track that has not been driven by a truck since the last wet.

sections.h: How a container gets to Longreach at all
p: There is no depot in Longreach and there is no scheduled service we can simply book a container onto. What actually happens is that your order waits for freight moving in the right direction, and depending on the week that is either a truck heading west along the Landsborough from the south-east corner, or a run coming across the Capricorn Highway from Rockhampton through Emerald and Barcaldine. Both are over a thousand kilometres of driving. That is why the honest lead time is one to three weeks and why we will not give you a firm morning until the truck is loaded and moving. What we will do is tell you where your container actually is in that process, rather than repeating a date that stopped being true a week ago.

None of that means you get treated as an afterthought. It means the ordering conversation matters more than it does anywhere closer in. Ring 1300 467 776 with the property or the street address, the size you want, what it is for and any date you are working toward, and we will tell you what the next realistic run looks like. If we need to hold your container in the yard for ten days to put it on sensible freight rather than chartering a truck, we will say that and explain what it saves you. If you need it faster than that, there is usually a way, and it will be a dedicated trip with the cost that goes with it.

sections.h: Downs country ground, dust and heat
p: Two things work on a container out here, and neither of them is rain. The first is ground movement. Self-mulching black soil swells and shrinks through the year and does it unevenly, so a container set straight onto the dirt will settle a corner at a time and go out of square. Once the four corner castings stop sitting at the same height the frame starts working against itself and the doors are the first thing to tell you. Sleepers or concrete pads under the four corners, levelled across both diagonals, prevent all of it for the price of an afternoon. Done on the day it lands it is an hour's work with materials that travel on the same truck. Left undone, the fix means lifting the container off again and emptying it first.

The second is heat. A steel box in a Longreach summer gets seriously hot inside, well beyond what most people expect, and the air inside carries whatever moisture came in with the last humid change. Vents let the heat move and give the moisture somewhere to go, which is why they matter more here than on the coast, not less. Fit them before the container travels. It also pays to think about what is going inside: aerosols, batteries, some chemicals and anything with a temperature rating on the label do not enjoy a closed container in February. If the contents are heat-sensitive, tell us and we will talk about vents, roof colour and where on the block the container should sit relative to afternoon shade.

sections.h: One trip out, so get the order right
p: The single most useful piece of advice for a Longreach order is to treat it as a one-shot exercise. Everything is easy while the container is standing in our yard. Vents, a lockbox, shelving, tie-down points, a personnel door, a repaint out of shipping-line livery, a second set of doors at the far end if you want to load from both sides. All of that is a routine job here and a genuine project once the container is sitting on a property four hundred kilometres past Emerald. Grade is worth settling at the same time. If the container is going to hold anything that has to stay dry for years on a property, ask for cargo-worthy, which is checked wind and watertight before it is loaded. The grades page runs through the differences.

The same applies to size and configuration. Two 20ft can go to two different sheds and are easier down a station track than one 40ft, but a 40ft is the better answer if you want machinery length under one roof and the approach can take it. High cube gives you an extra three hundred millimetres of internal height for the same footprint, which matters if you are stacking. Think it through, and use us for it. We have put enough containers into western Queensland to know which questions actually change the outcome, and the phone call is free. Tell us what the container is for and how long it has to last out there, and the right specification falls out of that rather than out of a price list.

faqs.q: How long is the wait for a container in Longreach?
faqs.a: One to three weeks, and we will not pretend otherwise. There is no depot in Longreach and no scheduled service to book onto, so your container travels when freight is moving that way, either west along the Landsborough or across the Capricorn from our Rockhampton depot through Emerald and Barcaldine. Both routes are over a thousand kilometres. The more warning you can give us, the better the odds of it riding out on freight that is already going rather than a truck chartered for one box.

faqs.q: What happens to delivery when the downs get wet?
faqs.a: It stops, and it stops for longer than the rain lasts. Mitchell grass downs soil holds water rather than shedding it, so roads get closed to heavy vehicles after rain and stay closed until they dry and are reopened. Nobody at our end can work around a closure. We build extra time into western bookings through the wet months and we will ring you with where your load actually is rather than leaving you guessing.

faqs.q: How hot does it get inside a container out here, and does it matter?
faqs.a: Hot enough to matter. A closed steel box sitting in a Longreach summer builds serious internal temperature through the afternoon, and anything with a temperature rating on the label will feel it. Vents fitted before the container travels let the heat move and give trapped moisture somewhere to go. Where the contents are genuinely heat-sensitive, we will also talk about roof colour and siting the container where it picks up afternoon shade. Say what is going inside at the quote.

faqs.q: Can you deliver to a station out of Longreach, or only into town?
faqs.a: Out to properties as well, but it is planned carefully. We need to know how far off the bitumen you are, what the track surface is, what condition the grids and floodways are in, whether there is firm truck-sized turning room at the shed, and when the track was last graded, since freshly graded surfaces have no bind and will not hold a loaded truck. If the last stretch is doubtful, we set the container down on the hardest ground we can safely reach and you shift it in with a tractor when it suits.

locations.line: Emerald is the most workable of our inland runs, and the reason is two hundred and seventy kilometres of sealed Capricorn Highway between it and our Rockhampton depot. That is one solid day rather than a fortnight of waiting for freight to line up. What it does not solve is the ground. Central Highlands cracking clay behaves the same as it does anywhere else on the black soil: superb when dry, hopeless when wet, and it will move a container out of square inside a year if the thing is sitting straight on the dirt.
locations.uses: chemical, drum and spray storage on the irrigation blocks around Lake Maraboon and the Nogoa, packing shed gear and bin storage for the citrus, grape and melon growers on the Emerald irrigation area, spare parts and tooling for contractors servicing the mines at Blackwater, Gregory and Capella, secure lock-ups on small claims and camps through Rubyvale, Sapphire and Anakie, hay, lick and fencing gear on the grazing country toward Springsure and Capella, and site storage for builders and trades working the Emerald residential streets
access: Emerald town is an easy delivery. The streets are wide, there is room for a rigid truck to stand, and the industrial area toward the highway is laid out for heavy vehicles. Out on the irrigation blocks it is generally good going too, because those places are built around getting machinery in and out. What you get instead are channels, headland drains, siphon pipe along the rows and overhead spans to pump sheds, all of which sit in awkward places for a truck with the bed up. The other thing about irrigation country is that the soil is heavy cracking clay, so the surface that carried a spray rig on Monday can be a genuine problem on Friday after a storm, and the Nogoa catchment can push water across low-lying blocks well after the rain has moved on. The Gemfields are a different job altogether. Rubyvale, Sapphire, Anakie and the tracks running off them are unsealed, narrow, rutted and dusty, with tight turnarounds and blocks that are small, uneven and often surrounded by spoil heaps and old workings. A 20ft goes onto most claims. A 40ft frequently does not, and the honest answer on a lot of those blocks is a 10ft or 20ft placed where the truck can safely reach rather than where you would ideally like it. Bulldust in the dry and slick clay in the wet apply out there as well. On the mine and contractor side, the constraint is not the road, it is the gate: inductions, PPE, a booked delivery window, a register and often an escort to the laydown area. Tell us at the booking which of these three worlds we are delivering into and the day sorts itself out.

sections.h: Two hundred and seventy kilometres up the Capricorn
p: Emerald is served out of our Rockhampton depot, and that is what makes it different to the far western towns. The Capricorn Highway is sealed the whole way, it carries heavy vehicles constantly, and the run through Duaringa, Blackwater and Comet is a normal working day rather than an expedition. That is why a four to eight business day window is realistic for Emerald when Longreach is measured in weeks, and it is why we can be more flexible about a hard date here. It also means a second movement is not a catastrophe. If a unit has to be swapped or shifted, that is a day's run rather than a fortnight of waiting on freight, and it changes how flexible anybody can afford to be when something does not go to plan.

Inspection is worth mentioning, because it comes up a lot. Stock sits at the Rockhampton depot as well as at our Cornubia yard, and inspection at Rockhampton is by arrangement rather than a walk-in. Ring 1300 467 776 first and we will sort out a time and make sure the unit you are interested in is where you can actually look at it. If a day on the road to the coast is not worth it, which for most Emerald buyers it is not, photographs of the specific unit are available on request and go out before delivery, covering the corners, both ends, the roof and the floor inside. Depot stock moves around, so ring before you make the drive rather than after you arrive.

sections.h: The Gemfields, and storage on a claim
p: A container is close to the ideal structure for a small claim out at Rubyvale, Sapphire or Anakie. It locks properly, it keeps red dust off gear that dust would otherwise destroy, it does not need a slab or an approval process before it can be useful, and it can be lifted out and taken with you if the claim changes hands. Plenty of them out there are doing exactly that job for wash plants, pumps, hand tools, fuel drums and everything else that would otherwise live under a tarp. It is also real security for gear that spends long stretches unattended, which on a small claim matters more than most other considerations. A lockbox fitted over the handle before the container goes out is worth the small cost, because a padlock sitting exposed on a quiet block is an invitation.

The limitation is getting the truck there. The tracks off the main roads are narrow, rutted and short on turning room, the blocks themselves are small and rarely level, and spoil heaps and old workings take up the space a truck would want to use. A 20ft is the practical maximum on most claims and a 10ft is often the smarter answer, since it can go where a longer unit simply cannot. Before you order, walk the approach as if you were driving a rigid truck down it, look for where a twelve-metre vehicle would turn around, and take a couple of photos. Send those with the enquiry and we can tell you what will fit rather than sending a truck out there to find out.

sections.h: Cracking clay and the wet
p: Central Highlands black soil does exactly what black soil does everywhere. It cracks open through the dry and it takes up water and swells in the wet, and neither happens evenly across a block. Put a container straight onto it and each corner casting punches in a little further than its neighbour, the frame goes out of square and the doors start needing a shoulder. That is the single most common complaint about a badly placed container anywhere on this soil type, it costs almost nothing to prevent and it is a real job to fix afterwards. Irrigation blocks are the worst of it, because ground that is wetted and dried to a schedule will move on that schedule too, year after year.

The fix is four sleepers or concrete pads under the castings, bedded in and checked level both ways and across the diagonals. Leave the underside open so air can move and water gets away instead of ponding beneath the floor, and where the site falls, face the doors uphill so they are not being lifted every time. If the block sits low on an irrigation flat or down near the Nogoa, take the highest usable ground over the flattest and get the floor well up. Elevation is the only thing that genuinely protects what is inside. A container is not a barrier against rising water and should never be sold to you as one: once water is at the door sill it is through the seals, and an empty box with the doors shut carries enough buoyancy to lift and travel.

faqs.q: What is the wait for a container in Emerald?
faqs.a: Four to eight business days is normal. Emerald is served from our Rockhampton depot, about two hundred and seventy kilometres east on the Capricorn Highway, which is sealed the whole way and carries heavy vehicles daily. That makes Emerald a far more predictable run than the towns further west. Crane bookings, a fit-out like vents or a lockbox, and wet weather on black soil are the usual reasons a date moves. Tell us if you have a fixed deadline.

faqs.q: Can you get a container onto a claim at Rubyvale or Sapphire?
faqs.a: Usually, with the right size. The tracks out there are narrow, rutted and short on turning room, and the blocks are small, uneven and often ringed with spoil heaps and old workings. A 20ft is the practical maximum on most claims and a 10ft is frequently the better choice because it goes where a longer unit cannot. Send a photo down the track, and another taken from the spot itself with the surrounds in frame, and we can tell you what will fit before a truck leaves Rockhampton.

faqs.q: Is a container safe storage on a low block near the Nogoa?
faqs.a: As a store, yes. As protection from rising water, no, and nobody should tell you otherwise. Once water is at the level of the door sill it is past the seals, and an empty container with the doors shut has enough buoyancy to lift and move. Elevation is what saves the contents. Take the highest usable ground on the block rather than the most convenient, stay off the path water takes when it runs across the site, and set the unit up on pads so the floor sits well up. Done that way it is excellent long-term storage.

faqs.q: Can you deliver into a mine site or a contractor yard near Blackwater or Capella?
faqs.a: Yes, provided the site requirements come to us before the truck leaves. An induction, PPE, a register at the gate, a booked window and somebody to lead the truck in are all standard and all easy to organise ahead of time. None of them can be organised with a driver already sitting at the boom at seven in the morning. Send through the site contact, what is required and the window you have been given, and it becomes a straightforward job.

locations.line: Everything about a Moranbah delivery is shaped by two things: the Peak Downs Highway, and whether the far end is a mine gate or a house. Stock comes from our Mackay depot, which means the Eton Range climb, then Nebo, then the run out across the Bowen Basin. That part is routine. The gate is where jobs go sideways, because a laydown area inside a mine lease is not a driveway you can just back into, and none of the paperwork can be sorted out with a driver already sitting at the boom.
locations.uses: tool cribs, consumables and spares storage in contractor laydown yards, secure lock-ups staged for shutdown crews who need everything in one place for a fixed window, dust-proof storage for filters, hoses, fittings and rigging gear, overflow storage for the camps and accommodation villages around town, gear storage for trades and small businesses working out of the Moranbah industrial area, and household and site storage on the residential streets where a garage lost the argument to a boat and a work ute
access: In town, Moranbah is a straightforward delivery. It is a planned town, the streets are wide, the blocks are regular and there is room for a rigid truck to stand and set up out the front of most houses. The industrial area has proper frontages and hardstand. The complications are elsewhere. The run in from Mackay climbs the Eton Range, which is a serious piece of road for a loaded truck and is subject to restrictions and closures from time to time, and it is one of the reasons we quote a window rather than a morning. Through the wet season the Peak Downs Highway and the roads around Nebo can go under, and when that happens nothing moves inland until they open. On the mine and contractor side, access is a process rather than a turn-off. Site induction requirements, a gate register, PPE, a nominated delivery window, a light vehicle escort from the gate to the laydown area, sometimes a permit for the vehicle itself. Laydown yards are often tighter than they look on a plan, with lay-down stacks, containers already in place and no straight run for a tilt bed, which is why a crane truck is frequently the sensible option out there rather than a tilt. Ground is the last piece. The Bowen Basin gives you heavy black soil in the flats and red gravel country on the rises. Both are excellent when dry. The black soil is a genuine problem after rain and stays soft long after the surface has crusted over, so a laydown area that looks fine can still be soft two hundred millimetres down. Tell us where the container is going, who controls the gate and what the surface is, and the job goes in first time.

sections.h: Up the Peak Downs Highway and over the range
p: Containers for Moranbah come out of our Mackay depot rather than from the south-east, which is a good deal shorter than most people assume and is the main reason a four to eight business day window is realistic here. The route is the Peak Downs Highway, up the Eton Range and out through Nebo. It is a well-used freight corridor, but it is also a road that is affected by weather and by works, and the range section in particular is not somewhere anyone rushes a loaded truck. Roadworks along that corridor are close to a permanent feature and they cost time rather than stopping the job, which is part of why we quote a window instead of an hour. The other part is that the last leg is often inside somebody else's gate, and gates run to their own timetable.

The wet season is the honest variable. Through the summer months the highway and the roads around Nebo can close, and there is nothing to be done about that except plan for it. If your container is tied to a shutdown, a contract mobilisation or a crew arriving, order early enough that a week of weather does not sink the schedule. Inspection at Mackay is by arrangement rather than walk-in, so ring 1300 467 776 first if you want eyes on a unit before it travels. Photographs of the actual container are the alternative, available on request and sent before delivery. Order early and a wet week becomes an inconvenience rather than the reason a crew stands around waiting on somewhere to put their gear.

sections.h: Shutdowns, laydown and the mine gate
p: A shutdown is exactly the sort of job a container was made for and exactly the sort of job that goes wrong when the container is ordered late. The requirement is short, defined and immovable: everything in one lockable place, on site, from a fixed date, gone again afterwards. Hire suits that shape perfectly, because the asset is off your books the moment the crew demobilises and getting it off site is somebody else's job. Buying makes more sense where the container is going to live in a contractor yard permanently and serve one job after another. Where a run of shutdowns is coming through over a season, it is worth asking about a longer hire rather than making the same booking three times, since the container can simply stay put between them.

What actually determines whether the delivery happens on the day is the gate, not the truck. Site inductions, PPE requirements, a gate register, a nominated delivery window, an escort from the gate to the laydown area and in some cases a vehicle permit are all standard, and every one of them is straightforward when arranged in advance and impossible when discovered at seven in the morning. Give us the site contact, the requirements and the window at the booking. If the laydown area is tight or already stacked, tell us that too, because it is often the difference between sending a tilt-tray and sending a crane truck. Sites also have their own quiet windows, and landing inside one of those beats arriving at shift change by a long way.

sections.h: Black soil, dust and the wet season
p: Bowen Basin ground has two settings. In the dry it is hard, dusty and will carry anything you drive across it, and the only real issue is that fine red and black dust gets into everything not behind a seal, which is a large part of why so much gear out here lives in a container in the first place. In the wet the black soil flats go to grease and stay soft well below a surface that has crusted over and looks solid. A laydown area or a house block that reads as firm can still bog a loaded truck, and once a truck is down in Bowen Basin black soil it is a serious recovery. It is a day nobody gets back, and it usually takes a decent piece of the laydown surface with it.

For the container itself, the same soil movement applies as anywhere on cracking clay. It swells and shrinks through the year and it does it unevenly, so a unit sitting straight on the dirt will settle a corner at a time until the doors stop lining up. Sleepers or concrete pads under each corner casting, levelled across both diagonals, deal with it permanently. Where the container is going into a laydown that already has hardstand, that is easier again and worth using. Tell us the surface at the quote and we will bring what we need to set it up properly on the day. It costs a great deal less than lifting a container back off a bad footing six months later, when everything inside has to come out first.

faqs.q: How long does delivery to Moranbah take?
faqs.a: Four to eight business days is the normal window. Stock comes from our Mackay depot up the Peak Downs Highway over the Eton Range and through Nebo, which is shorter than most people expect. The two things that stretch it are wet season weather closing the highway or the roads around Nebo, and site access requirements that need arranging before the truck can be booked. If you are working to a shutdown date, order early.

faqs.q: Can you deliver into a mine site laydown area?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is regular work, but the site requirements have to reach us before the truck is booked. Inductions, PPE, a gate register, a nominated delivery window, an escort from the gate and sometimes a vehicle permit are all normal. None of it can be arranged with a driver already parked at a boom gate. Give us the site contact and the access requirements at the booking, and tell us how much room there is in the laydown, since a tight or already stacked yard usually means a crane truck rather than a tilt-tray.

faqs.q: Should I hire or buy for a shutdown?
faqs.a: Hire, in almost every case. A shutdown has a defined start and finish, so hiring keeps the container off your asset register once the crew demobilises and leaves the removal to us rather than to you. Buying makes sense where the container is going to sit permanently in a contractor yard and serve one job after another. Give us the window when you enquire and it gets quoted the way the job actually runs.

faqs.q: Will a container keep the Bowen Basin dust out?
faqs.a: That is one of the main reasons people out here use them. Cargo-worthy units are checked wind and watertight before we load them, and with the doors shut and the seals in good order they keep fine dust off filters, hoses, fittings and rigging far better than a shed with a roller door. Two things help: keep the door seals clean rather than letting grit build up in them, and have vents fitted so the box can breathe without leaving a door propped open.
